title: Girdhar Ki Kundaliyan
author: Girdhar Kaviray
tagline: A staff, a blanket, a crow and a boat: Girdhar’s proverbial verses on prudence, generosity and judging people rightly.

overview.intro: Girdhar Kaviray writes kundaliyas — short linked couplets of practical wisdom, close in spirit to Kabir’s sakhis but worldly rather than theological. The Sahitya Sagar selection moves through everyday objects and observations: a staff for difficult ground, a coarse blanket that protects finer clothes, the crow and the cuckoo whose voices differ though they look alike, friendships that last only while money lasts, a thin tree that fails in a storm, water bailed from a boat, and the measured conduct expected in a king’s court. The method is analogy: an ordinary thing is described precisely until its moral becomes impossible to miss.

learn.title: The kundaliya form and Girdhar’s method

blocks.text: A kundaliya is a short couplet form built for recitation, often opening with a recurring line that links one verse to the next. Girdhar uses it the way a craftsman uses a proverb: he takes something completely ordinary — a walking staff, a cheap blanket, a crow, a thin tree — describes it accurately, and lets the description carry the advice. The reader is never told to be prudent; the reader watches a boat fill with water and understands.

This is why the selection rewards close reading of its images. The advice is general, but the images are specific and physical, and the specificity is what makes the teaching stick. Where Kabir compresses theology, Girdhar compresses practical ethics, and both rely on a reader willing to finish the thought.

items: The staff is praised as a companion that helps one cross difficult ground and defends against animals or attackers.
A cheap, coarse blanket is valued because it protects finer clothes, can be carried as a bundle and can be spread at night.
The teaching is not about the objects themselves but about the wisdom of choosing what is reliable and useful.
Girdhar consistently prefers the sturdy and serviceable to the merely fine or impressive.

blocks.text: The staff and the blanket couplets establish the poem’s value system. Worth is measured by what something does, not by how it looks. A staff has no elegance, and a coarse blanket is cheaper than the fine cloth it protects, yet both earn Girdhar’s praise because both prove themselves in use. This is a moral argument disguised as a description of two humble objects.

learn.title: Crow and cuckoo: judging by voice, not appearance

items.meaning: The bird whose appearance resembles the cuckoo but whose voice gives it away.
items.context: Used to show that looks deceive and qualities must be tested.

items.meaning: The singing bird valued for its voice.
items.context: The contrast proves that people are valued for merit, not resemblance.
Thousands seek a person of merit; without merit, none is valued.
The one without gun finds no takers, however fine the appearance.

blocks.text: The crow-and-cuckoo couplet is the selection’s most quoted, and its logic is merciless. Two birds may look alike, but the world listens: it values the cuckoo for its song and dismisses the crow. Girdhar transfers the point to people immediately — thousands seek a person of real merit, and without merit no one is sought, however impressive the surface. It is a lesson in discernment offered to both sides: develop merit, and do not be fooled by appearances in others.

blocks.caption: Girdhar’s analogies for reliability
rows: Friendship that lasts while money lasts
A thin tree in a storm
Bail it out — put wealth to good use
Be measured, patient and slow to speak

blocks.text: The middle couplets turn from objects to human relations, and the tone hardens. Girdhar observes that much of the world’s dealing is self-interested, and that friendships often survive only while one party has money or can serve another’s purpose. His images match the observation: a thin tree offers no shelter in a storm, so do not mistake it for support. The counsel is unsentimental but not cynical — it asks for clear sight, not misanthropy.

learn.title: The boat and the wealth it warns about

items.text: If water rises in a boat, it must be bailed out with both hands.
items.note: The image is physical and urgent; a small neglect becomes a sinking.

items.text: If money accumulates at home, the same two hands should give it away.
items.note: Girdhar treats hoarded wealth as the moral equivalent of water in a boat — dangerous where it sits.

items.text: To do so, he says, is the wise person’s work.
items.note: Generosity is framed as practical wisdom rather than as charity or display.

blocks.text: The boat couplet is the selection’s ethical centre. By placing hoarded wealth beside water in a foundering boat, Girdhar makes an argument about use rather than possession: value lies in movement, not in storage. The advice is addressed to the prudent, not the saintly — give, because keeping is the riskier course. It also quietly answers the earlier couplets, since the person of merit is precisely the one who understands this.

Questions here favour explanation of individual couplets and short notes on the central idea. Because each kundaliya is self-contained, the safest preparation is to learn each image with its moral firmly attached: staff and blanket for usefulness, crow and cuckoo for merit over appearance, thin tree for unreliable support, boat for generosity, court for restraint. Strong answers paraphrase the image first and then state the teaching, rather than naming the moral without the picture that proves it.

items: Pair every image with its lesson so no couplet is explained with the wrong moral.
Quote the merit couplet accurately — it is the selection’s most examined line.
Treat the boat-and-wealth couplet as a teaching on use and generosity, not on poverty.

figures.caption: Figure: Six images, six lessons
figures.description: A grid of six panels. (1) A walking staff on rough ground — reliability. (2) A coarse blanket folded over fine cloth — protecting what matters. (3) Crow and cuckoo side by side — merit versus appearance. (4) A thin tree bending in a storm — unreliable support. (5) A boat bailing water with both hands — generosity over hoarding. (6) A measured visitor in a royal court — restraint and patience.

figures.caption: Figure: Merit and self-interest
figures.description: Two contrasting columns. Left: "Gun (merit)" — thousands seek a person of merit, the cuckoo is valued, the sturdy tree shelters. Right: "Matlab (self-interest)" — friendships that last while money lasts, the crow’s borrowed appearance, the thin tree that fails. A dividing line is labelled "Girdhar’s judgement".

keyPoints: A kundaliya is a short linked couplet of practical wisdom, built for recitation.
Girdhar’s method is analogy: an ordinary object is described until its moral is unmistakable.
The staff is praised for usefulness — it crosses difficult ground and defends against danger.
The cheap blanket is valued because it protects finer clothes and travels as a bundle.
The crow and cuckoo look alike but their voices differ, so the world judges by merit, not appearance.
The merit couplet says thousands seek a person of merit, and without merit none is sought.
Friendships that last only while money lasts are named as self-interested dealing.
The thin tree offers no shelter in a storm, an image of unreliable support.
Water in a boat and hoarded wealth are paired: bail the boat, give generously — that is the wise course.
examFocus: Central idea: prudence, generosity, humility and clear judgement, taught through everyday analogies.
Explain-a-couplet question: paraphrase the image first, then state the moral precisely.
Merit question: the crow-and-cuckoo logic proves people are valued for qualities, not appearance.

questions.prompt: What does the staff symbolise in Girdhar’s verse?
questions.explanation: The staff helps its owner cross difficult ground and defends against animals and attackers, so Girdhar advises carrying it — worth here is measured by usefulness.
questions.commonMistake: It is not a symbol of status or asceticism but of dependable, practical help.

questions.prompt: Why does Girdhar praise a cheap blanket?
options: It protects finer clothes and can be carried and spread at night
It is a mark of simplicity
It is given by a friend
questions.answer: It protects finer clothes and can be carried and spread at night
questions.explanation: The coarse blanket guards the finer cloth beneath it, travels as a small bundle and serves as a bed covering — practical virtues outweigh its low price.
questions.commonMistake: The praise is functional, not a moral celebration of poverty.

questions.prompt: What does the crow-and-cuckoo comparison teach?
options: People should be judged by qualities, not appearance
Birds are hard to tell apart
questions.answer: People should be judged by qualities, not appearance
questions.explanation: Though they look alike, the crow and cuckoo are distinguished by voice; Girdhar transfers the point to people, who are valued for merit rather than resemblance.
questions.commonMistake: The birds are an analogy for human judgement, not a lesson about ornithology.

questions.prompt: In the boat couplet, what is compared to water rising in a boat?
questions.explanation: Girdhar pairs rising water with hoarded money: both grow dangerous where they sit, and both should be bailed out — that is, put to generous use.
questions.commonMistake: The comparison is with stored wealth, not with danger from outside.

questions.prompt: What advice does Girdhar give about the thin tree?
questions.answer: That one should not rely on a thin tree in a storm, but seek a sturdy, deep-rooted support instead.
questions.explanation: The thin tree fails when it is most needed, so the image warns against mistaking an unreliable person or ally for real support.
questions.commonMistake: Extend the image to human relations — it is advice about choosing whom to depend on.

questions.prompt: What does Girdhar say about friendship and self-interest?
questions.answer: That many friendships last only while a person has money or can serve another’s interest, which he calls self-interested dealing.
questions.explanation: The observation is unsentimental: he asks the reader to judge friendships by how they behave in scarcity, not by their appearance in prosperity.
questions.commonMistake: He describes the tendency rather than condemning friendship itself.

questions.prompt: Explain the merit couplet — that thousands seek a person of merit, and without merit none is valued — and its significance.
questions.answer: Girdhar says that thousands seek a person of real merit, but that a person without merit finds no takers, whatever else they possess. The significance is twofold. For the individual, it is an argument for developing genuine qualities rather than cultivating appearances, since the crow cannot pass for the cuckoo once it opens its mouth. For society, it is an observation that the world’s seeking is rational: people pursue merit because merit is useful to them. The couplet therefore sits at the centre of the selection, linking the earlier warnings about appearance to the later counsel about generosity and conduct.
questions.explanation: Paraphrase the couplet, then read it from both sides — the duty to develop merit and the insight that the world recognises it — before naming its place in the selection.
questions.commonMistake: Do not reduce it to "be good"; the couplet is specifically about merit being sought and its absence being fatal.

questions.prompt: What is the teaching of the boat-and-wealth couplet?
questions.answer: That hoarded wealth, like water rising in a boat, grows dangerous where it sits, so surplus should be given and put to good use.
questions.explanation: Girdhar frames generosity as practical wisdom — the wise person’s work — rather than as optional charity, because keeping is the riskier course.
questions.commonMistake: Present it as prudence, not as a sermon on poverty or a condemnation of wealth.

questions.prompt: Describe Girdhar’s kundaliyas and show how their everyday analogies carry his teaching.
questions.answer: Girdhar Kaviray’s kundaliyas are short couplets of practical wisdom, each built on an ordinary object or situation. The staff is praised because it crosses difficult ground and defends against danger; the cheap blanket because it protects finer cloth and travels as a bundle. The crow and the cuckoo look alike but are told apart by voice, so the world values people for merit rather than appearance — thousands seek a person of merit, and without merit none is sought. A thin tree fails in a storm, an image of unreliable support, which turns the reader toward friendships judged by how they hold in scarcity. Water rising in a boat is paired with money accumulating at home: both should be bailed out with both hands, and generosity is named the wise course. Finally, conduct in a king’s court demands restraint, patience and measured speech. The unifying teaching is prudence — choose what is reliable, value merit over show, give rather than hoard, and speak with restraint.
questions.explanation: Move image by image, always pairing the picture with its moral, then state the unifying teaching so the answer is an argument rather than a list.
questions.commonMistake: Do not detach an image from its lesson; explaining the crow as a general comment on nature earns little.

questions.prompt: Girdhar advises judging friendships by how they behave when money is gone. Do you think this is wise or cynical? Discuss.
questions.answer: The counsel is best read as wisdom rather than cynicism, because Girdhar does not deny friendship — he asks the reader to test it. His observations are empirical: much dealing in the world is self-interested, and the thin tree offers no shelter precisely when shelter is needed. Judging an alliance by its conduct in hard weather is simply prudent, and it protects both parties, since a friendship that survives scarcity is the one worth investing in. Yet the poem also disciplines the judge: the same person is expected to be generous, to bail out the boat rather than hoard, and to speak with restraint in company. The test, in other words, applies to oneself as much as to others, which is what lifts it above mere suspicion.
questions.explanation: Take a position, support it with the self-interest and thin-tree images, then complicate it by noting that Girdhar demands the same standard of the reader — generosity and restraint — which separates prudence from misanthropy.
questions.commonMistake: Do not simply agree that people are bad; show that the couplet is about testing, not about condemning.
